$comment: Where the subject sits on each accepted plate in docs/art/renders/, so that anything cropping a plate crops it around the subject instead of around the middle of the file. Read by tools/lib/framing.mjs; consumed by tools/build-cards.mjs (the card windows) and tools/build-data.mjs (the explorer thumbnails).
note: A plate is a whole drawn page - docs/art/prompts/ asks for A4 proportions and says card crops are taken from the plate later. A card window is not that shape, so something has to be thrown away, and the only question is what. `subject` says what may not be: the head, the hands, and the gear the card names. Everything outside it is scenery the crop may spend.

format.subject: [x, y, w, h] as fractions of the plate, 0..1 from its top-left. Draw it a little loose - the crop grows this box out to the window's shape, it never shrinks it, so a tight box only means more scenery comes with it.
format.focal: [x, y] as fractions of the plate: the one point the picture is OF. A face, nearly always; on a vehicle, the wheelhouse or the driver; on a monster, the eye. Optional, and new plates should have one - see docs/art/09-framing-and-composition.md. Subject says what may not be cut; focal says what the crop is aimed at, and the two do different jobs. Without it the crop centres on the subject box, and the middle of a standing figure's bounding box is their sternum.
format.focalTargetOverride: [x, y] as fractions of the WINDOW, if this plate should not use the default focalTarget below. Rare - a plate that needs its own target usually needs a better subject box.
format.note: Prose, for the next person holding the pen. Not read by anything.

focalTargetNote: Where a focal point lands in the window: centred across, a little above the middle down. That is where a reader looks first and where a face belongs. The crop slides to put the focal point here, as far as the subject box allows - the subject always wins.
padNote: Breathing room added around the subject before the box is grown to the window's shape, as a fraction of the subject's shorter side. Keeps a head off the window rule.

character-chr-01.note: Corin at the stump, lacing a boot - head, both hands and the staff top.

character-chr-02.note: Berga crouched over the pan; the pan is the card, so the box runs down to it.

character-chr-03.note: Sylvae reading - head, the open herbal, and the hand writing in it.

character-chr-04.note: Tilly on the crate: head, the gourd under one arm, the hand chalking the tally.

character-chr-05.note: Ruk seated at the haft - head high, both hands and the axe head across the middle.

character-chr-06.note: Elspeth reading a vial against the light; the open case is the other half of her.

character-chr-07.note: Havik in the motion works - head, both hands in the gear, the lamps left.

character-chr-08.note: Old Mother Keswick shelling into the bowl. The cat comes along below if there is room.

modification-storm-shutters.note: The three propped shutters, the open one showing its hide lining, its tacks and the tarred rope round the rebate, with the mallet and the keg. One per cent off the bottom takes the foot of the mallet head; the lining, which is the thing this card is actually selling, stays whole.

modification-sweep-rig.note: The gooseneck pivot with its drawn pin, both spars end to end, the laced sail and all four crew handles. Nothing is spent: at 78% of the page height the rig clears the flat window's 80% ceiling, so the card and the thumbnail both keep it whole. The quiet deck above the upper spar is what bought that.

modification-warded-hold.note: The crate lid standing proud, the crowbar bent under it and plainly not moving, and the nearest two marks in the end grain. The box is 94% by 72% and the ink fits whole at both windows with room over. What the crop spends is the deckhead arch above and the run of floor planking below, both of which are there to say small cargo hold and neither of which the card names; the row of crates carrying the rest of the marks runs off the right margin as the brief allows.

monster-ash-drake.note: Snout at the near corner to the far curve of the tail - the whole animal, laid diagonally across the page. Both windows grow it downward, which brings the bent pick in whole on the card and spends only its haft on the thumbnail. The smoke off the nostril is on the left margin and survives at card width.

monster-barrow-troll.note: Both shoulders wall to wall, the torc and the broken sword in the chest thatch, and down to the toppled stone. A 0.96 window on an A4 page can be at most 0.736 of it tall and this troll wants 0.742 from crown to the stone's base, so the box hands the pad three pixels of turf dome and three of buried stone - neither of which anyone will miss. The thumbnail keeps head, shoulders and grave-goods and leaves the stone to the card.

monster-cinder-wolf.note: Ear tips to front paw, muzzle to tail: the whole animal, with the banked coals behind the ribs inside it. Wide enough that both windows grow it downward, which is what brings the smoke off the spine and the burnt rings in the grass along for free. The shepherd's crook is scale and the card can spend its lower shaft.

monster-deepwater-maw.note: The eye and the ring of teeth. The ship on the horizon is scale, not subject - it goes.

monster-dust-devil.note: The funnel and the wagon it is emptying, whole; the debris trailing off the top may be spent.

monster-forge-wight.note: Hood down to the near foot, and out to the right of the tool row: the wight, both hands, the riveted splice on the cart rail, and the mended tools laid out like offerings. Focal is the empty hood - the head is a void and the void is the face. The card takes the whole tableau; the thumbnail keeps hood, hands and splice and lets the tool heads sit on the bottom edge.

monster-gravel-wyrm.note: The arch of plated back and the blind maw at the end of it.

monster-hoarwyrm.note: Tail tip to snout - all three undulations - and down past the horizon so the wyrm is seen to be flying over something. Whole at 0.539 of the page, which is the first plate in this deck small enough that both windows take the animal entire and nothing has to be traded. The white band and the reindeer leaving it are below any reachable crop; they are the story, not the subject. The box starts six thousandths below the tail tip and lets the pad carry it, because the lowest frost spikes on the ruff are the true bottom of the animal at 0.645 and the 5:4 thumbnail needs every pixel between the two.

monster-mire-strangler.note: Both drowned trees, the bundle hung between them, and the first fan of roots.

monster-reef-serpent.note: The head taking the offered fish, the coils on the beacon, the bow of the boat.

monster-rime-harpy.note: Head to talons, both wings. The nest at the foot of the crag is scenery.

monster-stone-boar.note: Rump to snout: the whole animal, because the boulder hide IS the card. The animal is 0.56 of the page tall and a 5:4 thumbnail can only hold 0.565, so the box stops just under the tallest dorsal spikes and lets the pad carry them - spend a spike tip before you spend the nose, which is the half of the picture the story is about. The oak, the furrow and the spilled basket are scale.

monster-storm-roc.note: The spread wings and the lamb; the sea stack below carries as much as fits.

monster-vhalrik-the-cinder-crowned.note: Crown down to the crossed forelimbs, wide enough to carry the wagon wheel. This plate ran its crown to the top margin rather than into the middle 70% the brief asked for, and MON-13 is a unique with a wordy rule, so its window is 1.10 and can hold only 0.643 of the page - the subject spans 0.79 and something the brief named had to go. The tips of the tallest horns go: the crown still reads as crown from 0.09 down, whereas a wheel cropped to a sliver reads as nothing at all.

vehicle-veh-01.note: Locomotive to last carriage, with the smoke above the stack.

vehicle-veh-02.note: The water tower and the ore train running away from it.

vehicle-veh-03.note: Old Smoke and her tender, wheels on the rail.

vehicle-veh-04.note: Hull and both masts to the mastheads.

vehicle-veh-05.note: The whole carrack, bowsprit to stern, mastheads in.

vehicle-veh-06.note: The lateen sail and the loaded hull under it.

vehicle-veh-07.note: The column of wagons, lead team to the last tilt, pennant included.

vehicle-veh-08.note: The wagons on the causeway and the reeds they are crossing.

vehicle-veh-09.note: All four switchbacks, the lead team at the top to the screw brake and its crewman at the bottom.

vehicle-veh-10.note: The courser at full gallop, nose to tail.

vehicle-veh-12.note: Horse and rider on the night road; the moon is spendable.

vehicle-veh-13.note: Driver and sled at the near end, the gang line receding to Drum, and the loose spare on the right.

vehicle-veh-14.note: The lantern on the stern bracket round to the bow, all five sails, down to the sea.

vehicle-veh-15.note: Stern to the chase gun, mast trucks down to the waterline. The 1.60 window cannot hold the whole page, so the foreground sea is what it spends.

vehicle-veh-16.note: Envelope nose to propeller, gondola and all four crew, down through the cloud bank to the far horizon.

vehicle-veh-17.note: Envelope crown down through the sail and the bow hinge to the gondola and the rowers.

talisman-tal-01.note: The knot at the top of the thong down to the three marked charms.

talisman-tal-02.note: The knot itself with its hanging loop.

talisman-tal-03.note: The disc and enough of the pooled chain to read as one.

talisman-tal-04.note: Both halves of the open locket - the portrait is the point of the card.

talisman-tal-05.note: The stone in its claws, and the plait it hangs from.

talisman-tal-06.note: Stopper to base of the flask, with the crystal caged inside it.

modification-compound-boiler.note: Both cylinders and the plainly different diameters that make it a compound, the receiver pipe and its lagging band between them, the crankshaft with its cranks, and the flywheel. A square plate against a near-square card window keeps the page, and the 5:4 thumbnail is the one that has to be paid: it holds 80% of the height and the ink wants 82%. The 2% is spent off the BOTTOM - the bedplate's lower lip and the shadow under it - rather than off the top, because the top is the two domed cylinder tops with their standpipes, and the difference between those two diameters is the whole of what the card says. The oil can and the long-spouted feeder on the bedplate survive at both windows.

modification-copper-sheathing.note: The sheet stood on end at full height, the fanned stack behind it, the spilled keg and the shipwright's hammer. The standing sheet is the product and its height is the whole point of the picture, so the 6% the flat window cannot hold comes off the bottom: it spends the tin snips in the corner, which are a scale prop the card does not name. The ghosted hull may run to the margins.

modification-fleetfoot-binding.note: Her face and both hands on the open hub, the knotted cord wound three times round the axle stock, and the crystal tied into the last knot. The leaning wheel is inside the box on purpose and not as scenery: the stock is drawn heavy, and the wheel off its hub with the trestles and the spanner is what makes this a wheelwright's yard rather than a gun on a carriage. Nothing has to be spent - 87% by 79% against the thumbnail's 80% of the height - so the straw, the grease pot and the spanner all survive the card window and only the last of them grazes the thumbnail's bottom edge.

modification-ice-runners.note: Both runners with their cast brackets and U-bolts, and the displaced wheel that says what they come off. Nothing is spent: at 74% of the height it clears the flat window's ceiling with room over. The spanner, the screw box and the tallow rag along the foot are scenery the crop may have.

modification-iron-ram.note: The ram on its cradle, the row of scarf bolts laid out beside it, and the sledgehammer leaning there for scale. One per cent off the bottom, which is the far end of the washer row; the ram itself is whole in both windows.

modification-keelbound.note: The midships scarf with the run of out-of-register marks along the grain, the alchemist's chalk hand and the bowl in the other, and the mana crystal in its wooden cradle at the lower right. Nothing has to be spent at either window: the box is 87% by 76% and the 5:4 thumbnail holds 80% of the height, so the ink fits whole and the pad gives up the difference. The ends of the keel run off both margins, which is what the brief set them aside for, and the standing water and the slip timbering behind are the scenery that lets them.

modification-salamander-grate.note: The grate stood on end with the heat flat between its bars, the bound shape strapped into its cradle underneath, and the fireman standing well back with his slice bar. The box is 93% by 80%, which is exactly the 5:4 thumbnail's budget, so the card window keeps the page and the thumbnail trims 2.4% off the BOTTOM. That is the tongs on the foundry floor, and they are the right thing to spend: the brief puts the tongs and the cooling trough beside the work and names only the grate, the bound shape and the slice bar as what may not be cut. The trough is at the right and survives both.

modification-spinnaker.note: The folded sail and the clew stretched out of it, with the spar and its bell fitting; the palm, the wax and the snuffer at the foot are scenery a flat window may spend.

people-dwarf.note: Pick over the shoulder, lamp in the other hand, head between them.

people-elf.note: The weaver at the loom - head and the sprig she is holding up to look at.

people-halfling.note: Yoke across the shoulders with a basket swinging at each end.

people-human.note: The builder with the maul up and the frame he is raising behind him.

item-leather-jerkin.note: The whole jerkin, shoulders to hem, with the belt and both skirt panels. Focal on the buckle. Drawn plate - measured off the picture, unlike its generated neighbours.

item-chain-mail.note: Collar to the split hem, both sleeves and the belt. Focal on the buckle. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-plate-harness.note: Both pauldrons, the breastplate and all three fauld lames. The bench below is scenery the crop may spend. Focal on the centre ridge. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-grappling-hook.note: All four flukes and their points, the shank, the ring, the thimble and the seized rope tail. Drawn corner to corner, so the box is 91% of the width: the ring runs out to 4% on the left and the sprung fourth fluke to 95% on the right. An earlier box called the left edge at 10% and the card window grazed the ring - measured again off the plate map, which puts it at 5%. Both windows now hold the whole of it. Focal on the crown where the four flukes leave the shank, not the middle of the box, which is bare bench. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-helm.note: Crown to the tip of the nasal, brow band and every rivet. Focal where the nasal meets the band. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-satchel.note: The body, both gussets, the flap, both buckled straps, both D-rings and the full loop of the shoulder strap. The loop is what makes this the widest box in the deck at 93% - it runs out to 2% on the left and 95% on the right, and it is named by the brief, so it is veto and not scenery. The top edge is the flap at 12%, not the 10% first guessed; that 2% is the whole reason the thumbnail holds this plate with nothing spent. Focal on the flap between the two buckles. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-shield.note: The whole disc, rim to rim, with the stapled split top-left. Focal on the boss. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-sword.note: Point to pommel, both quillons and the whole grip. The sword is drawn corner to corner with no margin, so the box is nearly the page: the card window holds all of it, and the 5:4 thumbnail cannot - it keeps the point and spends the pommel. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-travelling-cloak.note: The hood, the shoulder cape, the throat strap and toggle, the full drop of the folds and the whole hem. The trestle it hangs over is scenery on both sides and sits outside the box, so the crop may spend it and does. Focal on the hood and throat, high on the drop: the empty hood is what says travelling cloak, and a box round a full-length hanging garment centres on its knees. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-war-axe.note: Wedge and poll down to the knob, taking the beard and the binding. Focal on the eye where the bit meets the haft. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-bag.note: The whole bag - all four seams, the gathered neck, both cord tails and their knots, the belt loop and the darned patch. The drawstring swings out to 12% on the left and the box is loose to 10% to carry it. Both windows hold everything. Focal on the gathered neck rather than the body: the pleats and the cord are what say drawstring bag, and the round bottom is the part a reader can infer. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-bow.note: Both horn nocks, the whole stave and string, and the corded grip. A narrow upright subject on a square page, so the crop brings a lot of paper with it. Focal on the grip. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-war-hammer.note: Face and fluke across the top, both langets, and the haft down to the wrapped butt. Focal on the head where the langets start. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-coil-of-rope.note: The whole coil, the spliced eye, the whipped end and both hanging tails. Nothing is spent: a coil is a wheel, so the subject is nearly as wide as it is tall and both windows take it whole - the pad gives up the last 0.6% rather than any ink. Focal on the middle of the coil, where the hole is, because that is where an eye lands on a wheel of rope and centring on the box alone would aim at the same place by accident rather than on purpose. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

item-crossbow.note: Both prod tips and lashings, the string, the whole tiller to the butt cap, the nut and the hanging trigger. Focal on the nut. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

tile-manor.note: The house, gable to gable, with the balustrade and the four clipped trees along its front and the mounting block on the sweep. Nothing is spent by the CROP that matters - the rhombus window is 1.24 against a 3:2 page, so the full height is kept and 9.7% of the width goes, off a left margin that is balustrade tip and bare ground. The DIE is what costs here, and it costs the walled kitchen garden entirely: a rhombus keeps the upper LEFT and lower RIGHT lobes, and the garden was drawn into the upper right - the one corner this shape does not have. No crop saves it; all four aims tested keep 60% of the page ink to within 0.3%, so the only question was which things go. Shifted 3% left of centre against the two the shift does buy: the leftmost clipped tree and the left chimney stack, both of which the centred crop cut. The plate was drawn to the full page against a brief that asked for the middle 60% - that is why a quarter of the piece is bare gravel and why the garden was never reachable. Not fixable by aiming; noted for the redraw.

tile-sawmill.note:
The whole page. A triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate, so the crop spends nothing and the tile keeps the ink edge to edge - the answer the warehouse, granary, barracks, quarry and lumber camp all got, and for their reason: on this shape the crop is never where anything is lost.

What IS lost is the WATER WHEEL, and the die takes it - aim-solve measures a rectangle and reports that the ink fits, which is true and beside the point. Below the shoulder line a triad keeps only the middle half of its width. The wheel is drawn at 15%-28% across and 50%-68% down, which is outside that on both counts, and it goes but for the top of its arc. No aim reaches it: the crop has one per cent of freedom and the wheel is fifteen from the cut. Accepted rather than redrawn, because the brief asked for the crank shaft AND the pit wheel and the shaft is the half that survives - it runs along the top left with its iron collars, high on the piece where a triad is still full width, and it says water-driven without the wheel being there. Whole and inside the cut: the board roof and its frame, the blade on its carriage, the three chained logs on the deck, the sawdust and offcuts, and the stickered lumber stack.

The focal is the blade. It is the working end and it is the one thing on the plate that tells a sawmill from a cart shed at seventeen millimetres. For whoever briefs the next triad: a thing that must survive belongs above the shoulder line OR inside the middle half of the width - the wheel was outside both.

tile-shrine.note:
The canopy, the stone under it and the offerings at its foot. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, and all of it is spent off the LEFT. That was measured by proofing both, not judged - the plate is drawn LARGE on its page, the canopy spanning some 40% of the width with its outer columns close to the corners the hexagon trims, and where the crop sits decides how many of the four columns stand clear. Spent evenly the rear right column is clipped at the top and the roof slab loses its right corner: the piece reads as a canopy with a leg missing. Spent left, all four columns are whole from base to capital and the slab is whole with them.

What it costs is the approach of the beaten path at the far left, which the name band covers anyway. This is the cheapest 13.4% in the batch.

Whole and inside the cut: the four columns, the low pitched slab roof, the daylight going straight through under it - which is the whole point of an open canopy and the first thing a tight crop kills - the rough standing stone, the stepped base of three courses, the shallow bowl and the bundle of cut stems. The slab's back-left corner touches the upper-left cut and is not taken by it.

The focal is the standing stone. It is what the shrine is of; the canopy is only the thing built to shelter it. The band falls on the worn ring and the path, which is the ground the brief set aside for it.

tile-smelter.note:
The whole page, for the warehouse's reason - a triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate, so the crop spends nothing and the tile keeps the ink edge to edge. On this shape the crop is never where anything is lost.

This is the one plate of the four the DIE costs almost nothing, and it is composition rather than luck: the stack is drawn right of centre with its top well inside the upper margin, which is exactly what the brief asked for and exactly what the envelope wants. Whole and inside the cut: the stone stack battered inward with its open mouth, the tapping arch with the fire in it, the sand runner and the bar cast in it, the pot at the runner's head, the great bellows in the board lean-to with its nozzle through the wall, and the charging ramp of earth and timber running up the back. The ore heap on the right loses its outer half to the right lobe and still reads as broken rock; the black heap in the lower left goes under the band, which is the ground the brief set aside for it.

The focal is the tapping arch. It is the working end, it is the only lit thing on the plate, and it is what tells a smelter from a windmill or a kiln at thirty-seven millimetres - the stack alone is a tapering tower and could be anything.

tile-steelworks.note:
The brick shed with its six arched openings and its iron-framed roof, the coal heap with the plank run laid over it, the stacked ingots on the apron, and the chimney. A rhombus window is 1.24 against a 3:2 page, so the full height is kept and 15.5% of the width goes. All but half a per cent of it is spent off the LEFT - the crop keeps x 17.0%-99.5% - and that is the whole of the aiming decision here: the crop can start no further right than 17.5%, and every millimetre it moves right is a millimetre of chimney saved from the die. Measured the other way for comparison - the even spend puts the chimney at 78%-87% across the piece, where the rhombus has already fallen away, and takes most of its shaft as well as its cap.

What the left spend costs is the brick-walled bay and the pale spent-lime waste in it, entirely: the crop takes most of it and the lower-left lobe would have taken the rest. That is the cheapest thing on the plate to lose - the brief itself set that corner aside for the name band.

What is lost that is NOT cheap is the CHIMNEY'S CAP, and no aim reaches it. The stack is drawn at 73%-81% across and starts 2.6% down the page, which is outside the safe box on both counts, and a rhombus keeps the upper LEFT and lower RIGHT lobes - the manor's shape and the manor's problem. The upper-right diagonal cuts the stack at about 13% down, taking the corbelled top and one banded course and leaving the shaft running off the edge. Nothing about the aim can move it: the crop already sits as far right as the page allows, and there is only 2.6% of paper above the stack, so no crop can put ground over it. The brief said the chimney may be cut by nothing and the plate was drawn against that. Accepted rather than redrawn - one moulding survives at the cut and reads as a band, the shaft is still the tallest and blackest thing on the piece, and the shed, the arches, the coal and the ingots are all whole and inside the cut. Noted for the redraw: on a rhombus the tall thing belongs over the LEFT lobe, and nothing may touch the top edge of the page.

The focal is the near gable and the chimney foot together - the business end, and what separates this from the smelter at forty-six millimetres is that it is big, black and straight-lined. The band falls on the paved apron below the ingot stacks.

tile-timber-house.note: The house, its chimney and the woodstore lean-to. The plate arrived PORTRAIT (1054x1492) for a pair tile whose window is 1.73 wide, so only 40.8% of the page height survives: the foreground path and both fence runs are spent, deliberately, and the building keeps the band. At 33mm across, that fence was never going to read anyway.

tile-town-hall.note:
The hall on its open arcade, the outside stair and its hooded doorway, and the paved floor with daylight running all the way under it. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full width is kept and 13.4% of the height goes; it is spent off the BOTTOM, pinning the crop to the top edge of the plate, and only 1.4% of the ink goes with it - foreground cobble.

What the DIE takes is the BELL COTE, and no aim reaches it. The cote is drawn at 53%-65% across with its roof 2% down the page. A pair is two pointy-top hexes side by side, so the notch where they meet descends from the top edge to a quarter of the tile's height at exactly half-width, and at 60% across the tile does not begin until 15% down. The cote spans 2%-24% of the tile's height, so its base and the lower half of the bell survive and its own little roof goes. The crop is ALREADY hard against the top of the plate and a pair has no horizontal freedom whatever - the full width is kept, so there is nothing to slide - which is to say this was decided when the plate was drawn and not here. The brick house's chimney, exactly, and the same lesson: on a pair the tallest thing belongs over a hex peak, a quarter or three quarters across, never over the middle. Here it is at 60%.

Whole and inside the cut: the first-floor hall with its four tall mullioned windows, all six columns of the arcade with paper showing between them, the outside stair and the hood over its door, and the benches under the arcade. The arcade is the silhouette and it is untouched, which is why the loss above is worth accepting rather than redrawing.

The focal is the arcade rather than the doorway. There is no working end on a moot hall; what tells it from a house at 37 mm is that the building is standing in the air on legs, and that is a gap rather than a thing. The band falls on the paving and the foot of the stair, which the brief set aside for it.

tile-trading-house.note:
The counting house with the arched carriage entry through it, the beam scale on its stand, and the cart in the passage mouth. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, and here EVENLY - 5.2% off each end - which is a decision rather than the default.

It was pinned to the top first, the way the town hall is, and that put both the bound chest and most of the hand cart outside the cut. The even spend buys them back. What it costs is a CHIMNEY, and the chimney is the cheapest thing on this plate: it is not in the brief at all - the subject paragraph names the arch, the door, the shuttered bay, the cart, the scale, the bales and the chest, and the roof only in the wash line - and it is drawn at 53%-57% across, dead in the notch, so it was never going to survive whichever way the height was spent. An unbriefed thing already lost, traded for a briefed thing that was recoverable.

What the DIE still takes is the three corded bales and the scale's graded weights, drawn at 51%-62% across and below 76% down the page. The bottom notch rises from the bottom edge to three quarters of the height at half-width, which is precisely where they sit - the same corner the granary's scoop went into, and no aim reaches it either. Accepted rather than redrawn: the beam scale, its stand and its hanging pan are whole and inside the cut, and the bales were supporting that cue rather than carrying one of their own.

Whole and inside the cut: the two storeys and all six windows, the panelled door with its steps and iron handrail, the shuttered bay, the arch with its shadowed passage and the fence at the far end of it, the part-loaded hand cart, the beam scale and the bound chest.

The focal is the carriage arch - dark, dead centre, and the brief's own test of a trading house against a warehouse. The band falls on swept paving and the foot of the door steps, and covers neither the arch nor the scale.

tile-vineyard.note:
The whole page, for the sawmill's reason - a triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate and the crop spends nothing.

The die takes the SHEARS. They are drawn at 78%-90% across and below the shoulder line, which is the corner this shape does not have, and no aim reaches them either. Accepted rather than redrawn: the basket is the same cue doing the same job, it is four times the size, and it survives - it sits just inside the notch at the head of the bottom lobe, losing only its right edge to that notch. Whole and inside the cut: the vine rows running corner to corner, which is what makes the combed bands read at all at this size; the chestnut posts and the wire between them; the dry-stone terrace wall across the lower third with the fallen course re-laid in it; and the dry worked ground between the rows. Nothing on this piece is tall, which is the whole of what tells it from the hop garden.

The focal is the basket on the wall - the human evidence, and the only point on a plate of repeating rows that is a point rather than a texture. The band falls on the terrace wall, which is stone and nothing else.

tile-warehouse.note:
The whole page, near enough. A triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate, so nothing has to be spent and the tile keeps the ink from edge to edge - the one framing entry on this deck that is not a choice about what to lose.

The focal is the padlocked double door under the hoist beam, which is what the tile is of: it is the working end, and it is where the eye should land at seventeen millimetres rather than on the long dark side wall. Right of centre by design - the plate is drawn from thirty degrees above and thirty to the left, which puts the business of the building on the right and leaves the lower-left as the foreground grass the name band is printed over.

tile-alchemist.note:
The house with its pot chimney and its glazed oriel bay. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full width is kept and 13.4% of the height goes - and every bit of it is spent off the BOTTOM, with the subject box set to the window's exact height so that nothing, not even the focal, can slide it back down. The charcoal kiln's trick for the charcoal kiln's reason, and here it is worth the whole tile: the chimney's top pot is drawn about 5% down the page, so an even spend cuts it with the CROP before the die ever gets a look, and a bottom-pinned crop clears it with room over the smoke.

The die then wants the same thing and gets it. A pair is two pointy-top hexes side by side, and the tallest thing on the page belongs over a hex peak, a quarter or three quarters across, never over the middle - the brick house's lesson. The chimney is drawn at about 70% across, which is very nearly the right-hand peak, and it stands the full stack of clay pots with its thread of smoke above them.

What the bottom spend costs is the STONE MORTAR ON ITS BLOCK and the COVERED CROCK, both, and the doorstep of the house with them. The mortar and crock are the brief's own lower-left furniture and were always half under the band; the doorstep is a real loss and is the price of the chimney, which is not a close call - the brief says the pot chimney and the glassware are what name this tile, and a door names nothing.

Whole and inside the cut: the oriel bay jettied out on its bracket with the pear-shaped alembic and both retorts silhouetted against its glass, the crooked lean of the house, the dormer, the slate roof, the four mortared clay pots and the smoke, the walled yard, the bed of tall strange-leaved plants. The left hex is largely open ground, which is the plate's own doing rather than the aim's: the yard was drawn low and the piece would be better with something standing in that cell. Noted for the redraw.

The focal is the oriel bay. It is the only lit thing on the piece, it is the working end - the glassware IS the trade - and it is what tells this from a crooked house at thirty-seven millimetres. The band falls on the plant bed and the yard wall.

tile-apiary.note:
The five skeps on their bench under the shingle roof, with the smoker and pail at the end of it. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, 6.7% off each side, and this is the one plate in the batch where the spend costs nothing anybody would name - there is flowering grass on both edges and nothing else. Whole and inside the cut: all five skeps and the repeat of their domes, which the brief calls the entire silhouette; the plank bench and its posts; the roof; the bee scatter at the hive mouths; the smoker. The covered pail loses a sliver off its right, and to the DIE rather than the crop. Not shifted right to save it - that buys the pail at the price of the roof's left eave, and the roof is what makes this an apiary rather than five skeps standing in a field.

The focal is the middle skep. There is no working end on this one and no door: the subject is a row, and the middle of the row is the honest place to aim it. The band falls on flowering grass, which is what the lower half of this plate is for.

tile-barracks.note:
The whole page, near enough, and for the warehouse's reason: a triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate, so the crop keeps the ink from edge to edge and nothing is spent there. On this shape the crop is never where anything is lost.

What IS lost is the hexagon, and aim-solve measures a rectangle and cannot see it. The range is drawn corner to corner - the wording told it to run "towards the far corner", which is an instruction to span the diagonal, and it did - so the two ends of the building are the exposed parts. The far end sits high on the left, where a triad is full width and keeps it. The near end sits low on the right, where a triad has narrowed to its centre half, and that end loses its gable corner. That was accepted rather than redrawn: the rank of windows, the yard wall, the gate, the spear rack and the drill post are all inside the cut and whole, and the near gable is the one part of this plate the tile can afford to lose.

The focal is the gate and the spear rack beside it. The window rank is what makes this building regular, but regularity is a texture and a texture has no point to land on; the rack and the drill post are what make it military rather than a long house, and they sit together just inside the yard wall. Left of centre here, unlike the granary and the warehouse, because this plate runs the other way: the business of it is at the near end, and the near end is bottom-left of the roof ridge rather than right of it.

tile-brewery.note:
The brewhouse, its vented ridge, and the barrel rick and ramp running out to the right. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent off the bottom bar three per cent, and what goes is bare ground.

This is the best-composed plate of the five and it is worth writing down why, because the other four are all paying the same bill. The louvred cupola - which the brief calls the signature and the first thing to draw - is at 29% across. A pair's hex peaks are at a quarter and three quarters, and 29% is all but exactly on one: the tile reaches the top edge of the page there, so the cupola survives whole, steam and all. The town hall's bell cote is the same kind of object nine per cent further in, and the notch has most of it. Nothing else about the two plates differs.

Whole and inside the cut: the long louvred cupola along the ridge with steam standing out of its slats; the copper mash tun lit through the open doorway; the stone ramp down to the cellar hatch with two barrels rolling on it; the rick of six barrels chocked on their sides; the brick shell, its slate plinth and its four small windows.

The focal is the mash tun in the doorway. It is the working end, the only lit thing on the plate and the only copper thing, and it is what tells a brewhouse from a brick barn once the cupola has been read as a roof vent. The band falls on the hop sack and the heap of spent grain at the lower left, the ground the brief set aside for it.

tile-brick-house.note:
The house, its roof, the walled yard and the water butt, from the chimney pots down to the cobbles at the doorstep. Nothing is spent by the CROP: a 3:2 plate in a pair's 1.73 window keeps x 2.9%-99.3% and y 0%-83.4%, and all that falls outside is foreground cobble.

What IS spent is the CHIMNEY, and the die takes it rather than the crop - aim-solve measures a rectangle and says the ink fits, which is true and beside the point. A pair is two pointy-top hexes side by side, so the notch where they meet descends from the top edge to a quarter of the tile's height at exactly half-width. The chimney is drawn at 47% across and 2.3% down, straddling that notch at its deepest: the one place on this shape that keeps nothing. No aim can move it - to stand the chimney over a hex peak the crop would have to begin a quarter of a page off the edge of the paper. Accepted rather than redrawn: all four windows, the panelled door and its hood, the roof, the rear gable, the yard wall, the washing line, the gate and the water butt are inside the cut and whole, and the stack's base survives at the notch as a stub that reads as roofline. For whoever briefs the next pair - the tallest thing on the page belongs over a hex peak, a quarter or three quarters across, never over the middle.

The focal is the panelled door under its hood: the human end, and what tells a house from a shed at seventeen millimetres. Left of centre, unlike the warehouse and the granary, because this plate is not drawn thirty-and-thirty - the lit front face carries the door and the business of it, and the right-hand end is yard. The subject box pins the crop to the top of the page, so the focal here records what the picture is of rather than driving where it lands.

The name band falls on cobbled apron and the base of the front wall, and covers neither the door nor any of the four windows.

tile-granary.note:
The whole page, near enough. A triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate, so nothing has to be spent and the tile keeps the ink from edge to edge - the same answer the warehouse got, and for the same reason: on this shape the crop is not where anything is lost.

What IS lost is the hexagon, and no framing entry can argue with it. Below the shoulder line a triad keeps only the middle half of its width, and the proof says what that costs here: the wooden scoop goes entirely, and the base of the outermost staddle stone on each side goes with it. Both sacks, the ladder and the daylight gap under the floor are inside the cut and whole. That loss was accepted rather than solved - the plate would have to be redrawn smaller on its page to keep the scoop, and the scoop is the one item on it the tile can afford to lose.

The focal is the small hatch high in the gable that the ladder reaches: the working end, and the one thing that tells a granary from a shed at seventeen millimetres. Right of centre by design - the plate is drawn from thirty degrees above and thirty to the left, which puts the business of the building on the right and leaves the lower-left as the foreground grass the name band is printed over.

tile-harbour.note:
The whole page, for the warehouse's reason - a triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate and the crop spends nothing.

The die costs this plate very little, and again by composition: the brief asked for the quay to run from the lower left up and away to the right with the crane at the centre right, and the crane lands square in the wide band a triad keeps full width. The treadwheel, the crane house, the jib, the block and the hook are all whole. So is the vessel alongside, with its mast cut by the top edge exactly as the brief intended, and so is the flight of steps cut down into the water - which sits in the bottom lobe where a triad has narrowed to its middle half, and survives because the plate put it near the centre.

What the die takes is the COIL OF HEAVY ROPE, drawn at 8%-22% across and 70%-77% down: outside the middle half and below the shoulder, the corner this shape does not have. The crates lose their outer edge to the left lobe and read as crates anyway; both barrels are whole. The rope is the right thing to lose - it is the one item on the plate that the dock also has, so it carries no identifying weight here.

The focal is the treadwheel. What separates this from the dock at thirty-seven millimetres is that everything here is stone and heavy where the dock is timber and small, and the wheel is where that argument is won: it is the only machine in either piece, it is a big plain circle among coursed rectangles, and it is a point rather than a texture. The band falls on swept quay stone, which is the ground the brief set aside for it.

tile-hut.note: The hut from the chimney down to the grass line, with the chopping block and the split rounds. Nothing is spent: a square plate in a 0.87 window loses 6.7% off each side and there is nothing out there but ground texture. Focal on the doorway - the one flat black shape on the plate, and the thing the tile is of.

tile-winery.note:
The press house: the great timber screw press, the vats beside it and the barrel rack below it. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent off the bottom, and 0.4% of the ink goes with it.

This is the one of the five the DIE costs nothing worth naming, and it is composition rather than luck. The press stands at 51%-68% across with its head 12% down - under the notch's descent rather than in it - so the beam, the screw and the counterweight all clear the cut. Set that beside the town hall's bell cote at 60% and the difference is about nine per cent of the page's width.

Whole and inside the cut: the press entire - squared frame, the screw, the bed, the basket, and the stone hung from the beam above it - which the brief calls the tile; both shallow staved vats and the trough running between them; the stone rack two courses high with its eight barrels; the stone catch trough and its wooden spout; the piers and the tiled roof over the lot. No vines, which the brief was explicit about - the vineyard is its own tile.

The focal is the press basket and the foot of the screw. It is the working end, and at 37 mm an open shed on stone piers could be almost anything until the screw is read. The band falls on the stacked empty baskets and the swept floor at the lower left, the ground the brief set aside; the back, where the band is drawn hollow, keeps them.

tool-axe.note: Wedge and poll, the whole bit and its hollowed edge, and the haft down to the knob. Focal on the eye. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

tool-saw.note: Toe, the whole toothed edge, both saw nuts and the tote. A wide flat subject on a square page, so the crop brings paper above and below. Focal on the heel where the tote meets the plate. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

tool-pick.note: Both ends of the head - the drawn point and the mushroomed one - the wedged eye, and the haft to the butt. Focal on the eye. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

tool-hammer.note: Face and pein across the head, both wedges in the eye, and the haft to the butt. Focal on the eye. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

tool-scythe.note: Blade tip to collar, both nibs, and the snaith to its butt. A tall narrow subject on a square page, so the crop brings paper either side. Focal on the collar where the tang is bolted. Drawn plate - measured off the picture.

tile-orchard.note:
The whole page, for the sawmill's reason - a triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate and the crop spends nothing.

This is the one plate in the batch the DIE costs nothing worth naming either, and that is composition rather than luck: the brief asked for staggered rows corner to corner so the pattern would survive the hexagonal cut, and it does. Four trees are whole, two are clipped at the edges and read as trees anyway, and what the lower lobes trim is grass and windfalls. Whole and inside the cut: the goblet pruning and the clear trunks whitened at the foot - which is what says kept rather than grown - the ladder set up into the centre tree, the picking basket at its foot, and the windfalls under the next tree along.

The focal is the ladder. It is the only made thing on the plate and the only straight line on it, so it is both what the eye lands on and what tells a worked orchard from scrub at seventeen millimetres. The band falls on open grass, which is the ground the brief set aside for it.

tile-palisade.note:
The toothed run corner to corner, with the gate and its drawbar. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, and all of it is spent off the LEFT rather than evenly. That is the whole of the decision and it is worth the gate - the drawbar and its iron ring are drawn out to 97% across, so an even spend cuts the bar in half and leaves the gate as two plain leaves. Spending left puts the ring inside the piece with room to spare, and the gate barred across is what makes this a defence rather than a paddock fence.

What the left spend costs is the head of the ditch and the leftmost few logs. The ditch was going to the band regardless - the brief set that corner aside for it - and at 20.7 mm, the smallest piece in the set, a ditch was never going to read as anything but shadow.

Whole and inside the cut: the axe-pointed tops running edge to edge, which the brief calls the entire silhouette and which is the one thing that had to survive; the gate, its two leaves, the drawbar and the ring; the plank walkway on its braced uprights with the rail above; the bank grass along the near side. The short ladder goes to the upper-left cut, and it is the one named thing here drawn outside the safe box.

The focal is the gate. There is no building on this tile and no working end in the usual sense, but a wall is read by its opening, and the gate is the only made thing on a plate that is otherwise a repeat.

tile-pasture.note:
The fenced run: the thatched field shelter, the trough on its gutter, the gate on its stone post, and the stock between them. A rhombus window is 1.24 against a 3:2 page, so the full height is kept and 13.5% of the width goes, 6.8% off each side. Spent evenly, and that is a real choice rather than the default - the alternatives were measured. Spending it all off the left buys the fourth sheep and costs the shelter's left third, and the shelter is the only built thing on the plate and the whole of what separates a pasture from an open field; spending it off the right costs the shelter outright.

What the DIE takes is the fourth sheep, which is drawn at 75%-88% across and below the shoulder on the right - the corner a rhombus does not have. Cheap: the brief asked for four sheep because a flock is a repeat, and three sheep and a cow still read as a flock at forty-six millimetres. The top-right run of fence goes with it, and the fence still carries three sides of the piece, which is what the brief wanted it for.

Whole and inside the cut: the shelter with its thatch and its poles, the gate and its stone post at the foot, the trough with water in it and the wooden gutter feeding it, the cow, three sheep at three different angles, and the worn tracks between trough, shelter and gate - which are the second thing after the fence that says this ground is kept rather than wild.

The focal is the cow. It is the largest single animal, it is the only piece of colour on a grey-green plate, and on a tile with no building to aim at it is the one point that is a point rather than a texture. The band falls on grass and the bottom rail of the fence.

tile-quarry.note: The whole page. A triad window is 0.99 against a square plate, so the crop spends nothing and the tile keeps the ink edge to edge - the same answer the warehouse, granary and barracks got, and for the same reason. The DIE is the only thing that cuts: a triad keeps a wide band across the top and only the middle column below about 45%, so the spoil run in the lower left goes. That is the ground the brief already named as the band s to cover, so it costs nothing. The windlass at the derrick s foot is clipped where the right lobe falls away; the derrick, the slung block, the drilled face with its wedges and the barrow of chippings are all whole.

tile-rail-depot.note:
The whole page, for the warehouse's reason - a triad's window is 0.99 against a square plate, so the crop spends nothing and the tile keeps the ink edge to edge. On this shape the crop is never where anything is lost.

The DIE is generous here and it is composition rather than luck: the brief asked for the rails to run the full width and out of both ends, and below the shoulder line a triad keeps only the middle half of its width - so the bottom lobe of this piece is nothing but permanent way. Ballast, sleepers and two rails, filling a whole cell. That is the best thing on the tile and no aim chose it; the plate was drawn with the track low and across, which is the one composition this shape rewards.

What the die takes is the BUFFER STOP, entirely, and the ballast heap and the stack of spare sleepers with it. All three are drawn in the lower left, outside the middle half, and no aim reaches them - the crop has one per cent of freedom and the buffer stop is twenty from the cut. Cheap, and cheaper than it looks: the brief itself set that corner aside for the name band, and a buffer stop is a rail END, which is the one thing this tile is not - it is where a town JOINS the network.

Whole and inside the cut: the board shed with both sliding doors and their diagonal bracing, the stone platform with its timber edge, the water tower on its four braced legs with the swinging spout and the rust in its seams, the hand crane on the platform edge, the crates and the hand barrow.

The focal is the water tower. The shed is a shed and the platform is a platform - at thirty-seven millimetres the tank on its legs is the only POINT on the piece that says railway rather than goods yard, and the track that says it louder is a texture running the width, which is not a thing an eye can land on. It stands whole in the upper right lobe with its conical roof inside the margin, which is what the brief asked for and what this shape needed.

tile-sand-pit.note: The riddle with its screened heap and the leaning shovel, the barrow at the head of the plank run, and the pit between them. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full WIDTH is kept and 13.4% of the height goes. It is spent off the BOTTOM, not evenly: the focal sits on the riddle, which pulls the window to the top of the page, and that is the right answer here because the bottom of this plate is loose pit floor and the top carries both pieces of furniture that say sand pit rather than hole. Measured rather than guessed - off the bottom keeps 71.1% of the page ink against 70.3% even and 68.2% off the top, and holds the riddle at 100% and the barrow at 87% where a true even spend leaves the barrow at 38%. The band falls on the pit slope, which is sand and nothing else.

tile-charcoal-kiln.note:
The clamp, its burnt ring and the cordwood stack. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page, so the full width is kept and 13.4% of the height goes. All of it is spent off the BOTTOM, and the subject box is set to the window's exact height so that nothing - not even the focal - can slide it back down. That is the whole decision, and it is worth 9% of the piece: the crown hole is drawn 15% down the page, and a pair's notch descends to a quarter of the tile's height at half-width, so where the crop sits decides whether the hole is in the piece or in the notch. Spent evenly it is cut and the dome is a mound of earth; pinned to the top edge it clears the notch by three per cent of the height and the tile has a chimney again.

What the bottom spend costs is the shovel blade and the front of the finished charcoal, both in the corner the band covers anyway. What the DIE still costs is the dome's left shoulder and the ridge of its apex, which straddle the notch at its deepest - the brick house's lesson wearing turf, and the same rule applies: the tallest thing on the page belongs over a hex peak, a quarter or three quarters across, never over the middle. Here it is at 56% and the crown hole at 60%, which is why one of the two survives and the other does not. Whole and inside the cut: the turf skin with its patches and cracks, all three vent mouths with fire in two of them, the crown hole, the cordwood stack, and the burnt bare ground the clamp stands on.

The focal is the large lit vent under the dome's face. It is the only fire on the piece and the only thing that says burning rather than a heap of earth; the smoke that used to do that job is above the page's own top edge and was never reachable.

tile-clay-pit.note: The pit and the standing water in it, with the clay drying on boards up to the left and the barrow on the ramp to the right. Deliberately NOT the even spend the sand pit gets. Wetness is the whole of what tells this tile from the sand pit at 37 mm, and on the even spend the die left the pool as a sliver in the bottom notch - the two pieces read the same. Dropped the window to a centre of 0.52: the water goes 69% to 78% of its area, and it is paid for out of the drying stack (74% to 66%) and the barrow (59% to 50%). The barrow is the right thing to spend, because a barrow on a plank run is exactly what the sand pit ALSO has - it carries no identifying weight here. The reeds survive whole at every setting, so the second wetness cue costs nothing.

tile-lumber-camp.note: The whole page, for the quarry s reason - a triad window is 0.99 against a square plate and the crop spends nothing. The stacks, the shear legs with the chain and hook, and the lean-to with the crosscut saw all sit in the wide upper band the die keeps; the skid track runs down into the lower lobe under the name band, which is the ground the brief set aside for it. The axe standing in its stump is on the left edge and loses its haft to the cut - it is the one thing here drawn outside the safe box, and it survives as a recognisable axe head.

tile-crop-cotton.note: The whole page - a field is texture edge to edge and there is no object standing in it to protect. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, and here it is spent off the LEFT, 11.9% off the left against 1.5% off the right. That is the whole of the aiming decision and the PICKING BASKET is what it buys. The basket is drawn well out at the right of the page; a centred crop takes it to the flat edge of the piece and past it, and the left spend brings it inside with the die's full width still under it - it sits between the corner vertices, where a hexagon has not begun to fall away. It is the human evidence on a plate of repeating bushes and it is the thing that tells cotton from any other white-flecked crop at seventeen millimetres, the bolls alone being small pale blobs. What goes off the left is the outermost bushes and bare ridged earth, which is the field again and costs nothing anybody would name. The band falls on dry earth and one bush at the lower left - a bush out of a dozen. Focal on the basket.

tile-crop-flax.note: The whole page, the crop keeping x 6.4%-93.0% and the 13.4% spent EVENLY, because there is no object on this plate at all - only the flower mass - and so nothing a lopsided spend could buy. What decides this tile is not the aim but the READ: flax and grain are both fine upright stems in ruled drills, and the one thing that separates them at seventeen millimetres is the cold slate blue flecked over the whole of this one against the ochre ears of the other. So the crop keeps that flecking edge to edge, which is the entire job, and any spend that traded flower for margin would be the wrong one. The trodden earth along the near edge sits in the lower left where the name band lands on it, which is the ground the brief set aside for it. Focal on the middle of the flower mass - a field of one crop offers no point to prefer, and saying so is more honest than aiming at an arbitrary flower.

tile-crop-grain.note: The whole page. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes, all of it off the RIGHT, and that is the one decision on this tile. It buys the LEFT POPPY. The poppies are the only points on a plate of ruled drills - the brief asked for two or three and got two - and this one is drawn close enough to the left margin that a left spend cuts it outright and a centred one pushes it into the outer twentieth of the piece; the right spend sets it about an eighth of the way in from the flat, clear of the band and legible as a red mark rather than a red pixel. What the spend costs is the outermost column of ears, which is the same ears again. The second poppy survives whole at the lower right, just above the band's end and just above the corner vertex where the hexagon starts to fall away. The stubble and trodden earth along the near edge stay in the lower left, under the name band, which is the ground the brief set aside for it. Focal on the left poppy.

tile-crop-hops.note: The whole page, the crop keeping x 6.4%-93.0% and the 13.4% spent EVENLY - a pole grid repeats and no column of it is worth more than the next, so there is nothing to buy by leaning. The poles run off the TOP edge and are meant to be cut by it, which is the one thing this tile is of: it is the only crop in this game drawn upward, and the height of the poles against every other field is its whole identity. That is also why the composition rule that governs a building does not govern this one - a hop garden drawn to sit inside the top margin would read as a hedge. The die takes the top and bottom points of the page and the poles survive it for exactly that reason, being drawn the full height rather than standing in the middle of it. The band falls on bare trodden earth and a grass tuft at the lower left. Focal on the near pole at its twine ties, the one place where the structure is a point rather than a texture.

tile-crop-vegetables.note: The whole page, the crop keeping x 6.4%-93.0% and the 13.4% spent EVENLY, and here that is a decision rather than a default: both things the brief names besides the cabbages sit at opposite edges - the bean row on crossed poles in the upper left, the leek row in the lower right - so a left spend buys one and cuts the other and a right spend does the reverse. The even spend keeps both, and both then clear the die: the beans below the upper-left diagonal where the hexagon has come out to full width, the leeks just above the lower corner vertex before it falls away again. What it costs is the outer bed on each side, which is more cabbages. The band falls on ridged earth, straw and one cabbage at the lower left - a head out of fifteen, and the affordable kind of loss. Focal on the large central rosette: this tile is of cabbages, and that is the one head big enough to be a point rather than a texture.

tile-dock.note:
The jetty on its piles with the boat made fast alongside, and as much of the bank as the band leaves. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes. All of it is spent off the LEFT, and that costs less than it looks - the left of this plate is the bank with the drying rack and the barrel on it, which is the ground the brief itself set aside for the name band, and the band covers that corner whether the crop does or not. Spending right instead would have cut the boat, and after the jetty the boat is what says dock. Whole and inside the cut: the decking and its rail, both bollards, the coiled rope, the chain, and the boat with the net heaped in it and its oar shipped. A fragment of the rack's crossbar survives above the band's top edge; the barrel is under it. Small and timber-built throughout, which is the whole of what keeps this from being read as the harbour.

The focal is the jetty head where the boat is made fast - the working end, and where the eye should land at seventeen millimetres rather than on the open water, which is rather more than half the piece by design.

tile-farm.note: The barn under its thatch, the cart shed with the cart backed into it, the muck heap and the trough, and the yard of ruts between them. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, and the focal on the barn pulls that off the BOTTOM so the thatched ridge keeps its clearance at the top edge. What it costs is the stone trough, which ends up largely under the name band in the lower left. That is a plate-composition cost and not an aiming one: a pair has only vertical freedom, so nothing about the aim can move a thing out of that corner. The barn, the cart and the gate are what the tile is read by, and none of them is in it.

tile-well.note: The wellhead, its shingled roof, the windlass and the bucket over the shaft, with the trough slopping over at the right. A single window is 0.87 against a square page: the full height is kept and 13.4% of the width goes. It is spent off the LEFT, all of it, and that was worth measuring - centring the crop clips the trough to 79% of its area, and the trough is a named part of this brief and the only thing on the page that shows the well is in use. Spending left instead puts it at 97% and costs the wellhead nothing (97% either way), because the left of this plate is the worn ground and path the brief already marked as expendable. This is the smallest piece in the set at 20.7 x 23.3 mm, which is why the name band takes proportionally the largest bite of any tile here; it falls on that same worn ring.

tile-oil-derrick.note: The lattice derrick and its crown block, the engine house and walking beam, both tanks on their bund, and as much of the slush pit as this shape will carry. A rhombus keeps the upper LEFT and lower RIGHT lobes - the manor's shape, and the manor's problem. The pit is drawn into the lower left, which is both the corner the die cuts and the corner the band covers, so it can never be wholly had. Shifted hard left, and that is measured rather than judged: the pit goes from 43% to 75% of its area and the derrick tower from 95% to 99%, paid for out of the outer tank (100% to 87%, a sliver off its right side). The tower is worth paying for - the brief calls its openwork against the paper the entire silhouette, and it is the only lattice tower in the set. The blackened ground around the well head survives whole and carries the oil where the pit itself is under the band. The upper-left lobe is bare grass: the plate's own empty ground, and no aim reaches it.

tile-market.note:
The shelter, its four posts and the open floor under it. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, taken off the bottom bar two per cent, and all of it foreground flags.

Whole and inside the cut, and this is the whole point of the tile: the daylight going straight through underneath the roof between the posts. The brief calls that gap the entire silhouette and says it must not be closed, and it is the one thing here that no part of the cut touches - it sits in the middle band where a pair keeps its full width. Also whole: all four posts, both trestles, the baskets and the crate stack, the beam scale hung from its tie, and the pole with the rolled awning lashed to it.

What the DIE takes is the finial and the apex of the pyramid roof, drawn at 53% across and 2% down - the notch again. It is the cheapest loss of the five: a hipped roof reads as a hipped roof without its point, and nothing about this piece is being carried by the roofline. The posts and the gap are carrying it.

The focal is under the roof, between the loaded trestle and the hanging scale. There is no door here and no working end - a market is a gap with furniture in it - so the honest place to aim is the middle of the furniture rather than any one piece of it. The band falls on the sacks and the flags at the lower left, which is the ground the brief set aside for it.

tile-mine.note: The adit with its cap piece and the tub on the rails in the left lobe, the winding gin over its collared shaft in the right, and the picking table of sorted ore below it. The piece reads ACROSS, which is what the brief asked a pair for and what the plate was drawn to. A pair window is 1.73 against a 3:2 page: full width, 13.4% of the height spent, pulled off the bottom by the focal on the adit mouth so the grass above the rise and the adit timbering both keep their clearance. The spoil tip runs out of the lower left under the name band, which is where the brief put it.
